query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of interstitial carbon (around 0.1–0.3 at.%) to tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys processed by stepwise thermo‐mechanical treatments will promote the in situ formation of uniformly dispersed, coherent nano-carbide precipitates. These carbides will act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion and enhance back-stress, thereby increasing strain hardening. The net effect is a simultaneous improvement in yield strength and ductility compared to undoped alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy manufactured via a stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation (SCCP) process that already yields high tensile strength (~2.15 GPa) with moderate tensile ductility (~15%) at ambient temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce trace amounts of carbon (approximately 0.1–0.3 at.%) during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: The effect is expected under the same thermo-mechanical SCCP processing conditions, with testing at ambient temperature and extended evaluation at elevated temperatures (up to ~800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of uniformly dispersed, coherent nano-carbide precipitates within the alloy matrix and at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent carbides will provide precipitation strengthening by pinning dislocations (via the Orowan mechanism) and creating localized stress fields that promote back-stress and enhanced strain hardening. This improved dislocation interaction delays plastic instability, thereby increasing both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an undoped tungsten-based refractory HEA processed under SCCP conditions, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit roughly a 10–20% increase in yield strength while maintaining or slightly improving tensile ductility (e.g., preserving ~15% or greater uniform elongation). High-temperature strength retention should also be comparable.
generation.baseline: The reference is the current state-of-the-art tungsten-based refractory HEA with SCCP processing that exhibits ultra-high strength (~2.15 GPa) and ~15% tensile ductility at ambient temperature.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected only if the carbon concentration is kept low (below about 0.5 at.%) to avoid coarse carbide formation and resultant embrittlement. The hypothesis applies within the processing window provided by SCCP treatments and may not hold in alloys with substantially different compositions or processing histories.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the observation of coherent nanoprecipitations in tungsten RHEAs (PMC10213035) and on studies showing that trace carbon can induce carbide formation with notable strengthening in refractory alloys (PMC7517255) as well as in interstitial-alloyed HEAs (PMC5227964). However, the quantitative effect of carbon on carbide coherence, dislocation interactions, and the precise balance of strength and ductility in tungsten-based HEAs remains somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory HEA samples via the SCCP process: one set with a controlled addition of ~0.2 at.% carbon and a control group without carbon. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM and APT) to verify the presence, size, and coherence of the carbide precipitates, then conduct tensile tests at ambient temperature and up to 800 °C.
measurements: Nano-carbide size, distribution, and interface coherence (via TEM/APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not show at least a 10% improvement in yield strength while maintaining or enhancing ductility relative to the undoped control, or if microstructural analysis reveals that the precipitates are incoherent or significantly coarsened (indicating embrittlement), then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, by incorporating the stepwise and independently controllable coherent nanoprecipitation strategy, a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy has been successfully developed to achieve an ultrahigh strength without compromise in tensile ductility. Through carefully designed thermo-mechanical processing, the SCCPs structure has been developed to induce coherent particle hardening from the nano-precipitation of both δ-lamella and γ″ particles within a bcc and fcc dual-phase matrix. This alloy exhibits a high tensile strength of 2.15 GPa and a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperatures, yet retains a tensile strength of above 1 GPa at temperatures of as high as 800 °C. We believe that our SCCPs design philosophy may provide a highly effective approach for the future development of other advanced materials with superior mechanical properties.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.
